title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
hook: an old rakshasa admits that he sees Rama behind every tree in the forest
carry: better to die by Rama's hand

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha told his king the hard truth. Pleasant things are easy to find, and Rama is dharma in bodily form.

Maricha has given his king the argument. Now he gives him something more personal: his fear. Let me tell you how I know Rama, he says. I was strong once, and proud. I went to break up Vishvamitra's sacrifice, and a boy, barely grown, shot me with one arrow and threw me a hundred yojanas into the sea. I lived. And I didn't learn, not then. It took a second meeting.
screen: `NOT AN ARGUMENT: A FEAR.` → `A BOY WITH ONE ARROW.` → `INTO THE SEA, ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Later, Maricha says, I came into Dandaka with two others, all three of us in the shape of deer, eating sages. Rama saw us and shot three arrows. My two companions died. I ran. Since then I've given all that up and live as a hermit. But I can't get away from him. I see Rama in every tree, dressed in bark, holding his bow. I see him in my dreams. Even words that start with his sound, ratna, jewel, ratha, chariot, frighten me. It's an astonishing confession from a villain, and a very human one. Then Ravana answers, and you can hear how this was always going to end. I didn't come for advice. A king's minister speaks when asked. Do as I say, or I'll kill you now. Maricha sees the trap. If I go, Rama kills me. If I refuse, you kill me. So he chooses. Better to die at the hands of an enemy like Rama, he says, than by my own king. And he goes. Now the week. Shurpanakha at the hut, and the brothers' jokes. The attack on Sita, and the wound that started the war. Fourteen, then fourteen thousand, and Rama standing alone. Akampana's escape. Ravana talked out of it, then shamed into it. And Maricha's warning, the rarest kind of advice, refused.
screen: `THREE DEER, THREE ARROWS.` · `I SEE RAMA IN EVERY TREE.` · `OBEY, OR I KILL YOU NOW.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `BETTER TO DIE BY RAMA'S HAND.`

segments.voice: Think of a fear that follows you around, the way Maricha saw Rama in every tree. Don't push it away or feed it; just name it softly. Then ask whether, in this room and this breath, it's actually here, and come back to the breath, the seat, the sounds.
Maricha, the rakshasa who confesses his fear, is threatened by Ravana, and agrees to go: better to die by Rama's hand than by his own king.
Your line: better to die by Rama's hand. Tomorrow, a deer made of gold. Another week, done.

screen: `DAY 567 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK FROM PANCHAVATI TO LANKA, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: THE GOLDEN DEER.`

howItsDone: Some Ramayana teachers use Maricha's confession, seeing Rama in every tree, as a striking example of how the mind dwells on what it fears, and some devotional readers see a strange kind of devotion in it.

original.note: Sanskrit mārīca: the rakshasa spared at Siddhashrama, who becomes the golden deer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maricha is a willing villain.
what it means: he warns, confesses his fear, and goes only under threat of death.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 38–41 hold his two memories of Rama, the 'ra' words that scare him, Ravana's threat, and his choice.

chat.says: Maricha knew the plan was doomed. Why did he still go along with Ravana?
options: Ravana threatened to kill him, so he chose to die by Rama's hand instead of his king's.
He secretly hoped the golden deer trick would finally let him beat Rama.
He thought Rama had grown weak in the forest and could be beaten now.
chat.meaning: Ravana said: obey, or I kill you now. Maricha saw death either way, and chose an enemy like Rama over his own king.

Maricha.meaning: the rakshasa who fears Rama and becomes the golden deer

Vishvamitra.meaning: the sage whose sacrifice young Rama guarded

yojanas.meaning: an old Indian measure of distance, many miles each

Dandaka.meaning: the great forest where the exiles live

recall: the sage who gave Rama Vishnu's bow
